holidays.name: National Neither Snow Nor Rain Day
holidays.description: A tribute to mail carriers who deliver through storms, heat, and everything else the weather throws at them. Write a letter, thank your postal worker, or just stand at the window and admire the mail truck.
holidays.origin: The day is an unofficial observance inspired by the famous line about couriers that is carved into New York City's James Farley Post Office building. The line is often linked to the postal service, though it is not an official motto.
holidays.funFact: The line comes from the ancient Greek historian Herodotus, who wrote about the mounted couriers of the Persian Empire. It ended up on a New York post office building in the early 20th century.

holidays.name: National Salami Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate the cured, garlicky, tangy sausage that stars on charcuterie boards and sandwiches. Slice it, fry it, or stack it on a cracker.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial food observance of unclear origin. It gives salami fans a reason to indulge in one of the world's oldest preserved meats.
holidays.funFact: The word salami is generally traced to the Latin word for salt, which makes sense because salt is what preserves the sausage and gives it its flavor.

holidays.name: National Acorn Squash Day
holidays.description: A salute to the dark green, ribbed squash with sweet, nutty orange flesh. It's often roasted in halves with butter and brown sugar, or stuffed with savory fillings.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial food observance of unclear origin. It lands at the start of autumn, when winter squash begins to appear in markets.
holidays.funFact: Acorn squash gets its name from its shape, which looks like a giant acorn. It belongs to the same species as many summer squashes, including zucchini.
